intrinsic_value_estimate: $71-$90 per share (central about $80). Method: capitalized owner earnings, the 'owner earnings' rule in Business analysis applied under the 'sensible price even if the future resembles the past' standard of brk-letter-1981#3. 1988 owner earnings estimated at about $2.30/share, conservative because all capex is deducted ($1,040M net income + ~$160M D&A - ~$12M undistributed equity income - ~$353M average capex, over ~365M shares). Assumes 10% growth for 10 years, then 5% forever, discounted at 9-10%. Pessimistic case (7% then 4%): $50-61. No-growth floor: about $23. Affiliate stakes (~$5.40/share at carrying value) are excluded as a cushion. The framework's literal Valuation rule (net working capital) gives only $0.05/share and is not used for a franchise business.
margin_of_safety: At $46.56 the price is 35% below value at a 10% discount rate and 48% below at 9%, in the case that cuts history by about a fifth. That meets the self-imposed hurdle of buying at least one-third below value with no loss in the pessimistic case (pessimistic value $50-61 is above the price). The margin rests on the franchise's growth, not on assets. It shrinks to about 6% at a 12% discount rate and about 21% on a $1.90 owner-earnings base.

key_reasons.reason: Return on equity is high and the core earns well above that on its own assets, without depending on leverage.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Business analysis: return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE of 19-21% every year 1976-83 with almost no debt; 27.2% in 1987 and a reported 33% in 1988. Soft drinks earned $1,432.5M operating income on $4,174M of identifiable assets in 1987 (about 34% pretax). Net debt/capital was 15.3% at YE1987 (ar-1986, ar-1987, upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: The soft-drink franchise has a durable moat: dominant and rising share, a brand consumers won't let the company change, and demonstrated pricing power.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Business analysis: durable competitive advantage, the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: US share over 40% (nine points ahead of the main competitor); world share over 44%; fountain share 59%, outselling the nearest rival more than 2-to-1. Coca-Cola classic became the #1 US soft drink after the 1985 reversal. Discretionary pricing under the CCE contracts; 1988 Latin America operating income +17% on +1% volume (ar-1986, ar-1987, upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: The core needs little capital, so most earnings are available to owners and growth costs little.
key_reasons.evidence: 1987 soft-drink capex $170M against $1,432M operating income; US concentrate gross margin about 63%. Consolidated owner earnings about $606-807M in 1987 and an estimated $2.30-2.82/share in 1988 (ar-1987, ar-1986).

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have produced far more than $1 of market value per $1, and buybacks have shrunk the share count at mostly sensible prices.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Management & capital allocation: each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983); buybacks only below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: 1981-88: $6.46/share retained against a $35.43 price gain (about $5.50 per $1; about $2.60 without the multiple expanding). 1984-85 repurchases at 11-15x earnings; average shares fell from 396.6M (1984) to about 365M (1988); 25.5M of a 40M-share program completed (ar-1986, ar-1987, upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: Able management in place, refocusing on the franchise, with mostly candid disclosure of one-time items and of the businesses that did poorly.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Management & capital allocation: honest, able management already in place; candid reporting (brk-letter-1979, brk-letter-1982 criteria)
key_reasons.evidence: Goizueta and Keough in charge since 1981. Unusual items quantified (+$0.68/-$0.33 in 1986). They admitted Columbia Pictures disappointed and Foods is 'in transition'. Entertainment reduced to a 49% CPE stake; soft drinks now more than 95% of operating income (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: The price assumes far less growth than the business has delivered, giving a 35-48% margin under the framework's standard for an outstanding business.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Valuation for an outstanding business at a sensible price (brk-letter-1987#18, brk-letter-1981#3); the literal net-working-capital rule (bpl-letter-1965) fails and is set aside for a franchise
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 price, 16.3x 1988 EPS of $2.85; it implies about 4-5% perpetual owner-earnings growth at 9-10%, against 11.6% a year net income growth 1976-88. International per-capita consumption is 16% of the US level. Management guides to mid-teens EPS growth for 1989 (prices, ar-1986, upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst is required; a passive minority stake fits because control is impossible and the operators are excellent.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Catalyst/timing: the market eventually reflects business results; Mr. Market is there to serve you (brk-letter-1987); 'non-voting partnership' in an excellent franchise (brk-letter-1981#3)
key_reasons.evidence: Market value about $16.5B; no pending corporate action; the ongoing buyback supports per-share value. The stock traded as low as $28.96 in October 1987, showing how far price can swing from value (prices).

key_reasons.reason: A large but not maximum position: the facts are clear and the franchise is durable, but value depends on growth continuing and on the discount rate.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Position sizing: concentrate when the facts are clear, up to 40% (bpl-letter-1965)
key_reasons.evidence: More than ten years of consistent reported results support a high probability the facts are right. No-growth value is about $23, and the margin is thin at management's 12% cost of capital, so the target is about 25% rather than 40%.

risks: Growth slows sharply. The no-growth value (about $23) is half the price, so the margin of safety depends on the franchise continuing to grow.

Currency: a weaker dollar flattered reported results by 27%, 16% and 10% in 1986-88. About 77% of soft-drink operating income comes from outside the US, and a stronger dollar would cut reported earnings.

Capital allocation outside the core: the history of diversification into entertainment and Foods, a 12% hurdle far below the core's return, a falling dividend payout and a higher 35% net debt ceiling could send cash into low-return uses.
Leverage and off-balance-sheet items: gross debt/capital 45.6% at YE1987; about $394M of guarantees and about $325M of recourse on CPE receivables.
Bottler economics: CCE handles about 45% of US volume and earns about 6% on its equity; formula pricing limits pricing in part of the US system.
Tax: the Puerto Rico exemption expires in 1995 (it lowered the effective rate by about 4-6 points).
Valuation sensitivity: at a 12% discount rate or a $1.90 owner-earnings base, the margin falls to 6-21%.
Information gaps: no 1988 annual report, no proxy (compensation and insider ownership), no long-term bond yield, no constant-currency figures.
what_would_change_my_mind: The 1988 annual report shows maintenance capex far above depreciation, or owner earnings well below about $2.00/share.
Constant-currency figures show international volume and profit growth mostly came from the weak dollar rather than per-capita gains.
Evidence the long-term government bond yield is well above 10%, which would make a 12%+ discount rate appropriate and remove the margin.
Sustained loss of US or world share to the main competitor, or proof that price increases are cutting volume.
The proxy shows management with little personal stock ownership and pay tied only to the stock price, together with new large acquisitions outside soft drinks.
A price drop to near or below about $35 with the franchise intact would argue for adding toward the 40% ceiling.
sell_triggers: Evidence I misread the business's economics: a lasting decline in soft-drink return on assets well below 25% pretax, or lost pricing power shown by falling unit margins.
A large move back into businesses without a moat (a major acquisition outside beverages) funded by the 35% debt capacity or by issuing shares on terms worse than the business value received.
Anti-owner actions: issuing stock below value, misleading reporting, or a material accounting surprise.
Erosion of the trademark: sustained share losses in fountain or food stores to the main competitor.
Under the 'forever' default for great businesses with great managers, a higher price alone is not a sell trigger.
